{{Short description|Kind of differential equation}}
{{Distinguish|Tanaka equation}}
In the [[stochastic calculus]], '''Tanaka's formula''' for the [[Brownian motion]] states that

:<math>|B_t| = \int_0^t \sgn(B_s)\, dB_s + L_t</math>

where ''B''<sub>''t''</sub> is the standard Brownian motion, sgn denotes the [[sign function]]

:<math>\sgn (x) = \begin{cases} +1, & x > 0; \\0,& x=0  \\-1, & x < 0. \end{cases}</math>

and ''L''<sub>''t''</sub> is its [[Local time (mathematics)|local time]] at 0 (the local time spent by ''B'' at 0 before time ''t'') given by the [[Lp space|''L''<sup>2</sup>-limit]]

:<math>L_{t} = \lim_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \frac1{2 \varepsilon} | \{ s \in [0, t] | B_{s} \in (- \varepsilon, + \varepsilon) \} |.</math>

One can also extend the formula to [[semimartingale]]s.

==Properties==
Tanaka's formula is the explicit [[Doob&ndash;Meyer decomposition theorem|Doob&ndash;Meyer decomposition]] of the submartingale |''B''<sub>''t''</sub>| into the [[martingale (probability theory)|martingale]] part (the [[integral]] on the right-hand side, which is a Brownian motion<ref>{{Cite book|last=Rogers|first=L.G.C.|title=Diffusions, Markov Processes and Martingales: Volume 1, Foundations|pages=30|chapter=I.14}}</ref>), and a continuous increasing process (local time).  It can also be seen as the analogue of [[Itō's lemma]] for the (nonsmooth) absolute value function <math>f(x)=|x|</math>, with <math> f'(x) = \sgn(x)</math> and <math> f''(x) = 2\delta(x) </math>; see [[Local time (mathematics)|local time]] for a formal explanation of the Itō term.

== Outline of proof ==
The [[Function (mathematics)|function]] |''x''| is not [[smooth function|''C''<sup>2</sup>]] in ''x'' at ''x''&nbsp;=&nbsp;0, so we cannot apply [[Itō's formula]] directly. But if we approximate it near zero (i.e. in [&minus;''ε'',&nbsp;''ε'']) by [[parabola]]s

:<math>\frac{x^2}{2|\varepsilon|}+\frac{|\varepsilon|}{2}.</math>

and use [[Itō's formula]], we can then take the [[Limit (mathematics)|limit]] as ''ε''&nbsp;→&nbsp;0, leading to Tanaka's formula.
